passage:
On a grey Saturday in Melbourne, Tuan found an old photo on his phone: him and Tomas on the fire escape of their student flat, eating pho from the place downstairs, both squinting into the sun. Tomas had moved to Adelaide for work a year ago. They'd traded likes since, not much else.
Tuan typed "Hey, how's things?" and deleted it. Too easy to answer with "good, you?"
Instead he wrote: "Found a photo of us on the fire escape with pho. I miss those Fridays. Free for a call Sunday evening?"
Tomas replied within ten minutes. "Mate. Yes. I still can't find decent pho here."
Later, scrolling, Tuan passed the group chat from his old five-a-side team, silent for months. He thought about reviving it, then just sent, "Great seasons, all of you. Thanks for them," and muted it without guilt.

qa.q: Where had Tomas moved for work?
qa.a: Tomas had moved to Adelaide for work a year ago.

qa.q: Why did Tuan delete 'Hey, how's things?'
qa.a: Feeling nostalgic for their Fridays, Tuan thought 'Hey, how's things?' was too easy to answer with 'good, you?' and wanted a message that would really reopen the friendship.

qa.q: Why did Tuan's second message work better?
qa.a: It named a specific shared memory and asked for a specific call time, making it easy for Tomas to say yes.

qa.q: How might the old teammates feel reading Tuan's thanks?
qa.a: They would likely feel appreciated rather than dropped, since Tuan closed that chapter warmly instead of letting it fade in silence.

grounding: Shows a young man reaching out with a specific memory and call time to a friend worth keeping, while letting another tie go with thanks.

passage:
In the reading room of the women's hostel, Sarika was meant to be revising pharmacology. Instead she was looking at two names on her phone.
The first was Irawati, who had sat next to her from Class 6 to 12 in Nagpur. They hadn't really talked since Irawati started law school in Pune. Sarika missed her laugh more than she'd admitted.
The second was Pallavi, from coaching classes, who had only ever messaged when she needed notes.
She typed to Irawati: "Remember Sunday poha at your Aaji's? I was thinking of it today. Call on Saturday?"
Then she opened Pallavi's chat, wrote, "All the best for your exams, and thanks for the coaching-days company," and let that be enough.
The warden walked past and tapped the desk. Sarika put the phone face down and turned a page. Ten minutes later Irawati's reply, a row of yellow hearts, lit up the screen.

qa.q: What did Sarika ask Irawati to do?
qa.a: Sarika asked Irawati to call on Saturday.

qa.q: What does Sarika feel about Irawati, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Sarika misses Irawati, especially her laugh, more than she'd admitted, which is why she reaches out with a specific memory. 🙂

qa.q: What is wise about how Sarika handled the two friendships?
qa.a: Sarika put effort into the friendship that mattered and let the other one go kindly with thanks, instead of forcing both or dropping both.

qa.q: What would change if Sarika had only sent Irawati 'Hi'?
qa.a: Irawati might have replied politely and nothing more; the named memory and set day make a real conversation far more likely.

grounding: Illustrates choosing which friendships to keep: a specific, warm invitation to one old friend and a kind, grateful letting go of another.

passage:
Dear Tejas,

I've been meaning to write this for weeks and kept waiting for the right moment. There isn't one, so here it is.

Yesterday I walked past the chai stall near our old college gate, and the man still had that chipped blue kettle. I thought of all our Sunday evenings there, arguing about films and planning lives we didn't end up living.

I miss that. I've missed it for a while, but I kept waiting for us to just drift back, and we haven't.

So: are you free this Saturday? I'll be at the stall at six. If you can't come, tell me a day that works.

And if things are different now, that's all right too. I'm grateful for those Sundays either way.

Noor

qa.q: What did the man at the chai stall still have?
qa.a: That chipped blue kettle.

qa.q: What does Noor feel when walking past the old chai stall?
qa.a: Noor feels nostalgic and a bit sad, missing the Sunday evenings, but also grateful for them.

qa.q: Which choice in the letter works, and why?
qa.a: Naming a specific place and time, Saturday at six, works better than a vague "let's catch up", because it gives Tejas something easy to say yes to.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel reading "if things are different now, that's all right too"?
qa.a: Tejas may feel relieved and free, not pressured, and so more likely to answer honestly.

grounding: Noor chooses to reach out with a specific invitation rooted in a shared memory, while accepting with gratitude that the friendship may have changed.

passage:
You asked how I handle old friendships after college. I'm Rekha, and I'll tell you about Sarita and me.

For about a year, we barely talked. Nothing happened. She moved to Kochi, I started work. I kept waiting for her to call, and I think she was waiting for me.

Then one night I found a photo of us at the Durga Puja pandal, faces covered in sindoor, laughing like idiots. I didn't write "hey, long time". I wrote, "I was thinking of that Puja night. Can we talk on Sunday?"

She called on Sunday. We talked for three hours.

But I'll be honest: I also had a friend from hostel, Lata, and when I thought about messaging her, I felt nothing. So I didn't. I just felt thankful for what we had.

Some you chase, some you let go with thanks. Both are allowed.

qa.q: Where had Sarita moved to?
qa.a: Kochi.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel about messaging Lata?
qa.a: Rekha felt no pull to reach out to Lata, only grateful and at peace about what they had, so chose to let that friendship go.

qa.q: What made Rekha's message to Sarita work?
qa.a: It named a specific shared memory and asked for a specific time, Sunday, instead of a vague "long time".

qa.q: How might Sarita have felt getting that message?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and happy, since she seemed to be waiting too, and she called on Sunday.

grounding: Rekha chooses which old friendships to revive with a specific message and which to let go with thanks, showing a mature response to fading friendships.

passage:
My roommate Lavanya had been moody all week, and on Thursday night I found out why.

She was sitting on her bed with her phone, typing and deleting. "It's Gautam," she said. "From school. We used to study together every evening. We haven't talked properly since he moved to Delhi."

She showed me her drafts: "Hi! Long time!" deleted. "How are you??" deleted.

Then she typed, slowly, "I was thinking of those evenings on your terrace doing maths. Can we talk on Saturday?" and sent it before she could delete it.

She put the phone face down and let out a long breath.

Gautam replied twenty minutes later: "YES. I miss that terrace." She laughed out loud.

I don't know what they talked about on Saturday. I only know she hummed all Sunday.

— Deepti

qa.q: When did Gautam reply?
qa.a: Twenty minutes later.

qa.q: How does Deepti seem to feel watching Lavanya send the message?
qa.a: Deepti seems curious and warmly supportive, and pleased when Lavanya laughs at the reply.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya's final message work better than her drafts?
qa.a: It named a specific memory, the terrace maths evenings, and asked for a specific day, so it felt personal and easy to answer.

qa.q: What might Gautam have felt on receiving the message?
qa.a: He seemed delighted and relieved, as his quick "YES" and "I miss that terrace" show.

grounding: Deepti, a roommate, observes Lavanya choosing to revive an old friendship with a specific message about a shared memory, and Gautam's warm reply.

passage:
Wednesday: Alka found an old photo of herself and Farida at the college canteen, two cups of chai, Farida laughing at something off-camera. They hadn't really talked in eight months. Alka typed "miss you!!" and deleted it. Too vague.

Friday: She wrote instead: "I was thinking of our Sunday chai at the canteen. Can we talk this weekend? Just half an hour?" She sent it before she could change her mind.

Sunday: Farida called at eleven. They talked for an hour and a half. It wasn't the same as before, but it was good.

Later that evening, Alka looked at her other old group chat, silent since June. She thought about those friends with warmth and a little sadness. She decided not everyone needed a message. Some chapters were just finished, and she was grateful for them.

qa.q: What did Alka find on Wednesday?
qa.a: She found an old photo of herself and Farida at the college canteen.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling on Sunday evening about the old group chat?
qa.a: She felt warm, a little sad and grateful, accepting that some friendships were simply finished.

qa.q: Why was Alka's Friday message better than 'miss you!!'?
qa.a: It was specific, recalled a shared ritual and asked for a clear, small plan, which made it easy for Farida to say yes.

qa.q: How might Farida have felt receiving Alka's message?
qa.a: Farida was probably touched and glad to be remembered, which is why she called on Sunday.

grounding: Over several days a young adult sends a specific message to revive one friendship and lets another go with gratitude.
